record.paper_title: Multi-D magnetohydrodynamic modelling of pulsar wind nebulae: recent progress and open questions
record.original_question: Where within the Crab Nebula are the gamma-ray flares produced, and can stochastic magnetic reconnection in thin current sheets near the termination shock or at the jet base accelerate particles to PeV energies on the observed hour-to-day timescales?

evidence.quote: Unfortunately, in spite of several attempts, no clear indication of a parent candidate location has been found yet, among the variable features observed in the optical and X-ray bands (e.g. the knots): none of these shows any special variation, during the gamma-ray flares.

The current favorite physical interpretation of the gamma-ray flares currently relies on acceleration of particles in an electric field beyond the ideal limit, since the constraint E ≤ B of relativistic MHD leads to an emission cutoff at approximately 200 MeV.

We cannot certainly determine the precise location for reconnection in the Crab nebula from this highly idealized model, but we have demonstrated that the reconnection process is able to occur on ideal time scales, independently on S_L and without invoking kinetic mechanisms, provided that during the current sheet dynamical evolution (thinning) the critical threshold of ε ∼ (S_L)^−1/3 can be reached.
Up to now the most plausible explanation seems to be violent stochastic reconnection events occurring in the TS region or at the jet base.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the Crab Nebula, a pulsar wind nebula powered by the Crab pulsar, in which day-scale gamma-ray flares above 100 MeV have been observed. Within the framework of relativistic ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), where the electric and magnetic fields satisfy E ≤ B and the synchrotron emission spectrum is therefore subject to a radiation-reaction cutoff near approximately 200 MeV, the observed flare emission requires acceleration of electrons/positrons to PeV (10^15 eV) energies on hour-to-day timescales in regions where the ideal MHD bound is locally violated.

(a) Identify the spatial site(s) within the nebula where the flaring emission is produced. In particular, determine whether the parent emitting region coincides with the termination shock region, the base of the polar jet, or some other localized structure (e.g. an optical/X-ray knot or wisp).

(b) Within a relativistic MHD model with Lundquist number S_L, decide whether stochastic (turbulent) magnetic reconnection in thin current sheets — driven by dynamical thinning of the sheets to an aspect ratio ε of order S_L^{−1/3} — and occurring near the termination shock or at the jet base, can:
   (i) operate on ideal (S_L-independent) timescales without invoking kinetic plasma effects, and
   (ii) accelerate particles up to PeV energies on the observed hour-to-day timescales,
   thereby producing gamma-ray flare emission consistent with the observed luminosities, durations, and spectral cutoffs above 100 MeV.
artifact.category_tag: Relativistic MHD and pulsar wind nebulae
artifact.status_search_result: The precise location of the Crab gamma-ray flares within the nebula has not been identified: searches in optical and X-ray bands have failed to single out a parent feature. Magnetic reconnection (often relativistic and/or stochastic) near the termination shock or jet base remains the leading candidate mechanism for accelerating particles to PeV energies on day timescales, but no consensus model fully accounts for the observed flare timescales, energetics, and emission above the standard ~200 MeV synchrotron cutoff. The question is therefore still open.

status_evidence.title: Extreme particle acceleration in magnetic reconnection layers — application to the gamma-ray flares in the Crab Nebula
status_evidence.snippet: Pairs accelerated to PeV energies within days; rapid acceleration cannot be driven by shocks; reconnection proposed as mechanism.
status_evidence.claim: Magnetic reconnection is invoked to explain PeV acceleration on flare timescales, but the precise emission site is not pinned down.

status_evidence.title: Gamma-ray flares in the Crab Nebula: A case of relativistic reconnection?
status_evidence.snippet: Flares could be associated with magnetic reconnection events in the highly magnetised relativistic plasma of the nebula.
status_evidence.claim: Relativistic reconnection remains a candidate, with the flare location still uncertain.

status_evidence.title: On the origin of variable gamma-ray emission from the Crab Nebula
status_evidence.snippet: Flares should come from a region with higher magnetic field, or imply 10 PeV electrons.
status_evidence.claim: The location and acceleration mechanism of the flares remain unresolved.
